title: 1 Samuel 25:14–31
context: One of Nabal’s young men warns Abigail, describing how David’s men had protected the shepherds and how Nabal insulted them. Abigail acts quickly, gathering generous provisions and riding out without telling her husband, while David vows to destroy every male of Nabal’s household by morning. David’s oath in verse 22 is printed in the WEB as “God do so to the enemies of David,” following the Hebrew; most Greek manuscripts read simply “David,” the usual form of a self-curse, and the wording “the enemies of David” is often explained as a scribal softening. Meeting David, she takes the blame on herself, names her husband’s folly, and appeals to David not to stain his future reign with needless bloodshed and self-avenging, reminding him of the LORD’s promise of a sure house. Readers in both traditions commonly treat Abigail’s intercession as a model of courageous, wise and godly restraint, and see God working through her to keep David from sin. Her words about David’s life bound in the bundle of life with the LORD are commonly read first as a confident statement of God’s protection over his chosen king.

verses.text: But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying, “Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master; and he insulted them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a young servant taking initiative to warn Abigail, recognizing the danger Nabal has created. Wisdom can come from unexpected places.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working through the servant’s report to set deliverance in motion. Both traditions commonly value the servant’s courage in speaking up.

verses.text: But the men were very good to us, and we were not harmed, and we didn’t miss anything as long as we went with them, when we were in the fields.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the servant’s testimony that David’s men were very good to them and did them no harm. The servant confirms David’s account.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the testimony as vindicating David’s request. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as exposing the injustice of Nabal’s response.

verses.text: They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the striking image of David’s men as a wall around the shepherds by night and day. Protection was real and constant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as showing David’s care for others even while he was a fugitive. Both traditions commonly read the verse as highlighting the ingratitude of Nabal’s refusal.

verses.text: Now therefore know and consider what you will do; for evil is determined against our master and against all his house, for he is such a worthless fellow that one can’t speak to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the servant urging Abigail to consider what to do, since evil is determined against the household. He also names Nabal as a worthless fellow who cannot be reasoned with.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the servant’s frank assessment as confirming the narrator’s description of Nabal. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as placing the burden of wise action on Abigail.

verses.text: Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two containers of wine, five sheep ready dressed, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail’s haste and generosity as she gathers bread, wine, sheep, grain, raisins and figs. Her quick action shows wisdom in a crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her generous gift as a fitting answer to David’s request and a means of peace. A seah has an approximate modern equivalent, and both traditions commonly focus on her generosity rather than exact quantities.

verses.text: She said to her young men, “Go on before me. Behold, I am coming after you.” But she didn’t tell her husband, Nabal.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Abigail sends the provisions ahead and does not tell Nabal. She acts independently to protect her household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her silence toward Nabal as a practical necessity given his character, described in verse 17. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse without treating it as a general rule about marriage.

verses.text: As she rode on her donkey, and came down hidden by the mountain, behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail riding down, hidden by the mountain, as David and his men come toward her. The meeting is perfectly timed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence in the timing of the encounter. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the moment when disaster may be averted.

verses.text: Now David had said, “Surely in vain I have kept all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that pertained to him. He has returned me evil for good.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David’s bitterness that he protected Nabal’s property in vain and was repaid evil for good. His sense of injustice is understandable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s words as revealing a heart inflamed with wounded pride. Readers in both traditions commonly see the danger of letting a just complaint turn into vengeance (compare Proverbs 20:22).

verses.text: God do so to the enemies of David, and more also, if I leave of all that belongs to him by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David’s oath to destroy every male of Nabal’s household as a rash and excessive vow. The vivid expression refers to every male.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a rash oath of total destruction that goes beyond just reprisal. Both traditions commonly read the oath as one David should not keep and is mercifully kept from fulfilling.

verses.text: When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got off her donkey, and fell before David on her face and bowed herself to the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail quickly dismounting and bowing to the ground before David. Her humility helps disarm David’s anger before she says a word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her posture as wise and respectful, recognizing David’s status. Readers in both traditions commonly see this as the beginning of a model intercession.

verses.text: She fell at his feet and said, “On me, my lord, on me be the blame! Please let your servant speak in your ears. Hear the words of your servant.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Abigail’s plea to let the blame rest on her, a costly act of intercession for her household. She stands between David’s anger and the people at risk.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her willingness to bear blame as a picture of mediation, which some readers in both traditions find suggestive of Christ’s intercession. Both traditions commonly hold that connection loosely while honoring her courage.

verses.text: Please don’t let my lord pay attention to this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him; but I, your servant, didn’t see my lord’s young men whom you sent.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail honestly naming her husband’s folly, noting that his name fits his character. Nabal means foolish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her candor as serving truth and peace rather than disloyalty. Readers in both traditions commonly note that she also explains she did not see David’s messengers.

verses.text: Now therefore, my lord, as the LORD lives and as your soul lives, since the LORD has withheld you from blood guiltiness and from avenging yourself with your own hand, now therefore let your enemies and those who seek evil to my lord be as Nabal.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail presenting the LORD as the one who has withheld David from bloodguilt and self-vengeance. She frames her intervention as God’s own work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her words as recognizing God’s restraining providence at work through her. Both traditions commonly read the verse as teaching that God guards his servants from sin by ordinary means.

verses.text: Now this present which your servant has brought to my lord, let it be given to the young men who follow my lord.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail offering her gift for David’s young men. Generosity replaces the stinginess that caused the crisis.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gift as making restitution for Nabal’s wrong. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a practical act of peacemaking (compare Proverbs 15:1).

verses.text: Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord fights the LORD’s battles. Evil will not be found in you all your days.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Abigail’s confidence that the LORD will make David a sure house because he fights the LORD’s battles. She speaks with remarkable insight into God’s purposes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her words as anticipating the promise of a sure house later given to David (2 Samuel 7:16). Both traditions commonly treat her as a wise woman who speaks truth about God’s plan.

verses.text: Though men may rise up to pursue you and to seek your soul, yet the soul of my lord will be bound in the bundle of life with the LORD your God. He will sling out the souls of your enemies as from a sling’s pocket.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers commonly read the image of David’s life bound in the bundle of life with the LORD as a vivid assurance of God’s protection over his life. They see it as encouraging David to trust God rather than take matters into his own hands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the image first as God’s secure keeping of David’s life, while his enemies are slung away like stones (compare Psalm 17:8). Some readers in both traditions extend it devotionally to God’s keeping of his people, holding that application with care.

verses.text: It will come to pass, when the LORD has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail looking ahead to the day when the LORD appoints David prince over Israel. She reminds him of the future God has promised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her words as confirming God’s purpose to raise David to kingship (compare 1 Samuel 13:14). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as reorienting David toward God’s promise.

verses.text: that this shall be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself. When the LORD has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail urging David to avoid the grief and offense of heart that needless bloodshed would bring. Restraint now will spare him regret later.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her wise counsel as protecting David’s integrity for his future reign. Both traditions commonly see her final request to be remembered as a humble close to a powerful appeal.
